subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
passage: It was Friday evening, the science chart on the water cycle was due Monday, and Elizabeth's little brother was banging a spoon on a pot in the next room. She unrolled the big sheet and stared at it. So much white. She sharpened three pencils, wandered to the balcony, came back and sat down with her chin on her arms. Her mother Sarita looked in. “Don't do the whole chart. Draw just one cloud, at the top left,” she said. Elizabeth drew a cloud. Then she added rain under it because that was easy. By bedtime she had three boxes drawn, and the white sheet no longer looked so large.

qa.q: What did Sarita ask Elizabeth to draw?
qa.a: Sarita asked Elizabeth to draw just one cloud, at the top left.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth sharpen pencils and wander to the balcony?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt overwhelmed by the size of the blank chart and was avoiding it, since she could not see where to begin.

qa.q: What worked in Sarita's suggestion?
qa.a: Naming one small first piece gave Elizabeth something to start on, and then the next piece felt possible.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel watching her daughter stare at the paper?
qa.a: Sarita probably feels concerned and patient, wanting to help without doing the chart for Elizabeth.

grounding: A child faces a large project, freezes and wanders off until a first small piece is in view.

subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
passage: On the call, Tanuja held up the social studies chapter, twenty-four pages, and let it flop on the bed. “I can't,” she told Rashmi. “Every time I open it I just see how much there is.” She had already refilled her water bottle three times. Rashmi, who was also stuck on the group map project, said, “Okay, I'll only do the border of the map. Tonight. You only read the first page and underline three words.” Tanuja groaned, but she opened to page one. The pencil felt light. By the time the call ended she had underlined five words and made a note of one question for tomorrow.

qa.q: How many pages does the chapter have?
qa.a: The chapter has twenty-four pages.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja refill her water bottle three times?
qa.a: Tanuja was avoiding the chapter because the whole size of it made her feel stuck and unable to start.

qa.q: What small step helped Tanuja begin, and what came next?
qa.a: Rashmi suggested reading only the first page and underlining three words; Tanuja then underlined five words and wrote a question for tomorrow.

qa.q: What might Rashmi be feeling about the group map project?
qa.a: Rashmi also feels stuck and a bit daunted, which is why Rashmi picked just the border to make a start.

grounding: A child sees only the size of a chapter and freezes until a first small piece is in view.

subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
passage: Come here, Jyoti, and leave that chart for a moment. When your mother, Leela, was ten, she had to make a solar system chart for school. The chart paper was huge and white. She stood in front of it for an hour, not drawing, just staring. Then she went and played with the calf. I, her grandmother, found her crying behind the shed. "It's too big, Nani." So we cut it into a plan. First only the sun, in the corner, big and yellow. That was all for day one. The next day, Mercury and Venus. By Saturday, all eight planets. She still has it.

qa.q: What chart did Leela have to make?
qa.a: Leela had to make a solar system chart for school.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when her grandmother found her behind the shed?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and hopeless, crying because the chart seemed too big to do.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Leela start?
qa.a: Deciding to draw only the sun on day one gave her a small first piece, which made the big chart feel doable.

qa.q: How did the grandmother see Leela's crying?
qa.a: The grandmother saw that Leela was frozen by the size of the task, not lazy, so she helped break it into small steps.

grounding: An elder tells how a child froze in front of a big chart until she was given a small first piece to do.

subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
passage: The summer holiday homework had to be finished by Monday, and it was Saturday. Pooja, eleven, sat at the kitchen table in their two-room flat while her little brother banged pots on the floor. Her history chapter was twenty pages. She flipped through it, sighed and went to the window. Then to the fridge. Then to the window again. Her cousin Lavanya, visiting for the weekend, sat beside her. "Just the first two pages. Find three dates." Pooja underlined 1757, 1857 and 1905. It took ten minutes. "Okay, two more pages," she said, a little surprised, and kept going despite the noise.

qa.q: How many pages was Pooja's history chapter?
qa.a: Her history chapter was twenty pages.

qa.q: Why did Pooja keep going to the window and the fridge?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed by the size of the chapter, so wandering around was a way to escape a task that seemed impossible.

qa.q: What small step helped Pooja get started?
qa.a: Lavanya's suggestion to read just two pages and find three dates gave her a first piece she could finish in ten minutes.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel after seeing Pooja keep going?
qa.a: Lavanya would likely feel pleased and relieved that her small suggestion got her cousin moving.

grounding: Illustrates a child who sees only the size of a long chapter and wanders off until given a small first piece.

subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
passage: Sunaina's science project chart was propped against the sofa in their Bhopal flat, still blank. It needed a drawing, labels, a table and a paragraph about plant cells. She looked at it, picked up a pencil and put it down. "I'll do it after dinner," she said. After dinner she went to watch her brother Hrithik play carrom. At nine, Hrithik saw her staring at the blank chart again. "What's the first thing?" he asked. "I don't know. All of it." He handed her a ruler. "Draw the border." She drew it. Then a big circle for the cell. By ten, the labels were done.

qa.q: What was the science project chart about?
qa.a: It needed a drawing, labels, a table and a paragraph about plant cells.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's picking up and putting down the pencil suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt stuck and overwhelmed, seeing the whole chart at once with no idea where to start.

qa.q: How did Hrithik help, and what could Sunaina do alone next time?
qa.a: He asked for the first thing and gave her one tiny task, drawing the border; next time she could name that first small step herself.

qa.q: What is it like for Hrithik to see his sister stuck?
qa.a: Hrithik seems to understand and want to help, calmly handing her a ruler rather than telling her off.

grounding: Shows a child frozen by a big project chart until someone points her to a tiny first step.

subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
passage:
"Avni, why are you lying under the table?"
"Because of the worksheet, Manjula aunty."
"What worksheet?"
"Thirty sums. Thirty! It'll take forever."
"Show me."
Avni crawled out and held up the paper. Three columns of sums, top to bottom.
"Hmm. That's a lot of sums."
"It's impossible."
Manjula aunty took a pencil and drew a line under the fifth sum. "How about just these five?"
"Only five?"
"Only five. Then you can go back under the table if you want."
Avni sat down. She did the first sum. Then the second. "These are easy ones."
"Are they?"
She finished the five and looked up. "Can you draw the next line?"
Manjula aunty drew another line after sum ten.
By dinner, Avni had done twenty. "The last ten tomorrow," she said, and went under the table anyway, grinning.

qa.q: How many sums were on Avni's worksheet?
qa.a: Thirty sums.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when she first looked at the worksheet?
qa.a: Avni felt overwhelmed and stuck, sure the thirty sums were impossible, so she hid under the table.

qa.q: What did Manjula aunty do that made the task possible?
qa.a: Manjula aunty drew a line after five sums, giving Avni a small first piece she could see and finish.

qa.q: How might Manjula aunty feel when Avni asks for the next line?
qa.a: Manjula aunty would probably feel pleased and quietly amused that the small pieces worked.

grounding: Illustrates a child who sees only the size of a thirty-sum worksheet and freezes, until a first small piece makes it doable.
